title: The month of Maghar
hookLine: in Maghar lovely are those who sit with the Beloved (Barah Maha, ang 135)

lines: TEA AT A LATE KITCHEN TABLE.
A FRIEND IN THE WAITING ROOM.
cards: Some good hours happen with nothing going on. A kitchen late at night, two people with tea, the dishes not done. A hospital waiting room where a friend just sits beside you and doesn't try to say anything wise.
A grandparent on a bench, holding a small hand, watching pigeons. None of it would make a highlight reel, but these can be the moments that stay.
Maghar, roughly mid-November to mid-December, is when the Punjabi cold comes in and people pull their chairs closer. Guru Arjan's Maghar stanza is about exactly that: sitting with.

teach.h: SOHANDEE-AA: LOVELY ARE THOSE WHO SIT.
teach.b: The stanza opens, in paraphrase: in Maghar, lovely are those who sit with the Beloved, the Lord. Sohandee-aa, lovely, shining. Baithrree-aah, those who sit.
That's all they're doing: not climbing, earning or proving, just seated beside the One they love, and the stanza says their beauty can't even be counted. Then the other side.

teach.h: APART FROM THE HOLY, WE STAY ALONE.
teach.b: Those who don't sit in the company of the holy stay alone. Their pain doesn't leave them, and they fall into death's grip. A whole Sikh practice lives inside that picture.
In the diwan hall of a gurdwara, people take off their shoes, cover their heads, bow, and then sit on the floor, together, at the same level. Nobody has a better chair.
They sit while the hymns are sung, sometimes a long time, sometimes saying nothing at all. That's sangat, the holy company, and in the Barah Maha it's where the bride finds the Beloved's presence.

teach.h: THE WEEK'S ROAD ARRIVES IN STILLNESS.
teach.b: Look back over the week and you can see the road. In Jeth she bowed. In Asarh she learned to keep Him near in the heat.
In Sawan she blossomed, in Bhadon she doubted, in Assu she longed and asked how, in Katak she stopped blaming.

Now, in Maghar, she simply sits. The stanza ends: in Maghar, those who worship the Lord are not born again into the round of coming and going. The long journey of the months arrives somewhere very still.

how: In the gurdwara, Sikhs sit together on the floor of the diwan hall, at one level, to hear kirtan; on the Sangrand of Maghar gurdwaras that keep the day read Guru Arjan's Maghar stanza from the Barah Maha.

o: the winter month of bathing at dawn
a hall where the sangat sits on the floor
the early-winter month of sitting together

games.q: the month of Maghar — tap the pairs.

s: in the Maghar stanza, the lovely ones are busy proving their devotion
they're simply seated with the Beloved; sitting is the whole picture.
the stanza says those apart from the holy company stay alone
it says their pain doesn't leave them; the sangat is where the bride finds company.
in a gurdwara's diwan hall, everyone sits on the floor at one level
nobody has a better chair while the hymns are sung.

games.q: the long road of the months has brought the bride to Maghar. what does she do there?
o: work harder to deserve the Beloved.
games.why: lovely are those who sit with the Beloved, the stanza says. after bowing, longing and owning her deeds, she simply sits.

practice: If someone you love is near, sit beside them now, no phone, no agenda; if not, bring one person to mind and sit as if they were next to you, their face, their hands, the way they settle into a chair.
Don't plan a conversation; just be with. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths, the One the stanza calls the Beloved.

wordCard.voice: Maghar. In the Barah Maha, Maghar is the month of sitting: lovely are those who sit with the Beloved, and the holy company is where we sit.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: sangat, the company, the congregation that sits together to sing and listen.

carryVoice: Your line: maghar: sit together. Tea counts; a bench counts. Day five hundred seventy-four, done.

sources.ref: Barah Maha, Raag Majh, Mahalla 5, the Maghar stanza (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 135)
